## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlfleetstack{5}{10}{15}{25}{35}{40}{70}{100}
\end{marginfigure}

_Why can an accurate, fast model still be unfit for deployment?_

In high-risk regulated settings, a model that cannot explain or document its behavior, support audit, or meet applicable discrimination rules may fail deployment review regardless of its accuracy or latency. Strong aggregate performance can conceal a pattern of errors concentrated among people with little power to challenge the outcome. Increasing throughput then increases the reach of that failure. A single-node evaluation can measure predictions, but it cannot establish whether every deployed version uses an approved decision policy or whether an affected person can obtain a correction. Across a fleet, records, models, interfaces, and organizational authority must remain connected as each changes. An explanation delivered too late may be useless to someone facing an immediate decision; retaining every detail indefinitely can create a separate privacy problem. Investigating an alert requires staff and evidence, while correcting a decision may require action across several dependent services. These obligations consume resources and can constrain deployment even when inference capacity is ample. They also persist after launch: a change in population, workflow, or model behavior can invalidate the evidence that originally justified operation. Responsible AI engineering makes those obligations part of the organization's daily operation, with resources and authority to act when measured behavior falls short. In C³ terms, responsibility is a coordination constraint: the fleet needs evidence and authority to decide when compute may run, when it must stop, and who can correct its consequences.

## The Governance Imperative {#sec-responsible-ai-introduction-responsible-ai-2724}

In 2018, Reuters reported that Amazon had abandoned an experimental hiring algorithm trained on historical resume data after discovering it systematically penalized female candidates [@dastin2018]. The historical records supplied a computable training objective, but reproducing patterns in those records was not the same as identifying qualified applicants fairly. The experiment exposed a mismatch between the learned objective and the legitimate hiring goal: historical success could encode unequal access rather than merit-based qualifications.

In the fleet stack shown in @fig-fleet-stack, responsible AI completes the Governance band\index{Fleet Stack!Governance band}, the point where the system meets the real world. The Infrastructure, Distribution, and Serving bands beneath it supply compute, data movement, distributed execution, and serving infrastructure. Within the Governance band, the Assurance row contributes security controls and robustness mechanisms, and the Governance & Sustainability row contributes sustainability budgets; responsible AI weighs that evidence and adds the constraints that determine why the machine runs and whom it serves, requiring owners to identify, assess, limit, and remedy harms from an otherwise correctly functioning system. Alongside the Fleet Law's accounting of execution time (@sec-vol2-introduction-fleet-law)\index{Fleet law!responsible AI stability}, responsible AI adds conditions for continued operation\index{Stability!responsible AI}: evidence that the deployment remains within its approved bounds and authority to intervene when it does not. The instability is concrete: a model that outputs toxic content erodes user trust (feedback-loop instability), a model that discriminates degrades its own future training data (distributional instability), and a model that leaks privacy invites regulatory shutdown (operational instability). Responsible AI therefore belongs in the objective function, not only as a constraint checked on the finished solution.

Production AI already has a systems agenda spanning architecture, infrastructure, data processing, security, and robustness [@stoica2017berkeley]. Responsible AI adds a distinct obligation: a service that remains available, secure, and accurate can still distribute harms unfairly or deny affected people a remedy. The hiring incident makes that distinction concrete. Fairness, transparency, and accountability therefore need measurable requirements and operating controls alongside the mechanisms that keep the fleet running.

::: {#dfn-responsible-ai-responsible-ai .callout-definition title="Responsible AI"}

***Responsible AI***\index{Responsible AI!definition} is the practice of designing, auditing, and operating ML systems to measurable fairness, safety, privacy, and accountability standards, translating ethical principles into verifiable system properties that constrain model training, deployment decisions, and operational monitoring.

1.  **Significance**: Responsible AI constraints impose real costs: fairness-aware training can lengthen training runs, real-time bias monitoring can consume serving-path latency, and on-demand explainability can require additional model evaluations or asynchronous worker capacity. At fleet scale, these safeguards must be budgeted like reliability or security controls. Conversely, a facial recognition system with a persistent subgroup error gap can affect millions of users before detection, creating regulatory and liability costs that dwarf the monitoring investment.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike AI ethics (which defines normative principles about what systems should do), responsible AI engineering defines technical mechanisms that enforce those principles, bias detection algorithms, differential privacy implementations, audit trails, and architectural guardrails that make compliance measurable and verifiable rather than aspirational.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that responsible AI is a final compliance review applied to a finished model. Postprocessing can satisfy selected metrics on observed outcomes, but threshold adjustment cannot repair an invalid target, unreliable labels, or missing information. Those defects may require changes to data collection, labels, or learned representations. The remedy depends on the source of harm; a final threshold check cannot substitute for investigating it.

:::

Responsible AI therefore constitutes a systematic engineering discipline with four interconnected dimensions: translating ethical principles into measurable system requirements, detecting and mitigating harmful algorithmic behaviors, addressing **sociotechnical dynamics**\index{Sociotechnical Dynamics!definition}[^fn-sociotechnical-system-etymology] that extend beyond individual systems, and navigating implementation challenges within organizational and regulatory contexts. Public frameworks such as the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) AI Risk Management Framework\index{NIST AI RMF!risk management}, ISO/IEC 42001\index{ISO/IEC 42001!management standard} and 23894, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development AI Recommendation, and the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization Recommendation on AI ethics all express this shift from abstract principles toward governable risk management, accountability, transparency, and human oversight [@nist2023airmf; @isoiec420012023ai; @isoiec238942023ai; @oecd2024airecommendation; @unesco2022ethicsai]. Privacy mechanisms, robustness techniques, and sustainability metrics provide the technical foundation for that integration. The responsible-AI framework combines those capabilities with bias detection algorithms, privacy preservation mechanisms, organizational governance structures, and stakeholder engagement\index{Stakeholder engagement!governance integration} processes, treating responsible AI as fundamental to sound engineering practice rather than as supplementary constraints applied to finished systems.

That integration is a significant infrastructure investment. @Sec-appdx-fleet-foundations-numbers-to-know supplies the production-scale fleet baselines and serving-capacity figures against which this overhead can be estimated, letting an engineer size the tax relative to the same per-accelerator throughput numbers used for raw serving. This cost is essential infrastructure to be provisioned, analogous to how security (@sec-security-privacy) and redundancy (@sec-fault-tolerance-reliability) are budgeted in distributed systems.

Treating fairness, transparency, accountability, and privacy as rigorous engineering specifications rather than abstract ideals transforms responsible AI from aspiration into practice. The systematic approach that follows maps these core ethical principles directly onto the mechanical stages of the machine learning lifecycle, turning each into a concrete design constraint with measurable criteria. The assurance lifecycle first establishes who may set and approve those constraints. Fairness metrics then make competing requirements measurable; deployment and monitoring turn the selected requirements into controls; sociotechnical analysis tests whether those controls remain effective in use.

### The governance and assurance lifecycle {#sec-responsible-ai-governance-assurance-lifecycle}

A model registry can prove which weights reached production, but it cannot prove that the deployment was justified. That judgment requires a chain of evidence connecting the deployment context to affected people, foreseeable harms, measurable requirements, implemented controls, accountable owners, and the authority to launch or stop the system. Responsible AI therefore needs an assurance lifecycle\index{Assurance lifecycle!evidence requirements}: a repeatable operating path that converts normative commitments into reviewable claims and keeps those claims valid as the system changes.

The lifecycle begins before model selection. Teams first define the intended use, prohibited uses, affected parties, operating environment, and decision consequences. They then identify harms and requirements, including subgroup performance, privacy, security, robustness, sustainability, human-oversight, and contestability obligations. Some controls are implemented locally; others are inherited from data providers, foundation-model vendors, cloud platforms, or downstream operators. Each inherited control needs an interface contract stating what the supplier guarantees, what evidence supports that guarantee, and which residual risks remain with the deploying organization.

Constraint selection needs an explicit division of authority. Domain experts and affected parties identify consequential harms and acceptable uses; policy and legal specialists identify applicable obligations; engineers determine what can be measured and enforced. The accountable launch authority approves the resulting criteria and records unresolved disagreements. A convenient metric or an available implementation does not authorize the engineering team to choose whose errors matter most.

The resulting assurance case is not a single compliance document, but a versioned set of linked artifacts that structure accountability across the system lifecycle. At its foundation sits an explicit *claim* defining the property required for a specified use and operating envelope. An *argument* articulates how operational controls and empirical observations justify that claim, drawing on *evidence* from reproducible evaluations, audits, access logs, documentation, and user research. These claims and arguments hold only under stated *assumptions* regarding environmental, population, supplier, and workflow boundaries. To ensure operational authority, every assurance case specifies an accountable *owner* empowered to block launch, restrict use, or require remediation, governed by an explicit *invalidation rule* that defines the measurable performance change, distribution shift, or operational incident that expires prior approval and triggers reassessment.

This structure prevents a common category error. A fairness dashboard, privacy accountant, red-team report, or carbon inventory is evidence for a bounded claim; none is itself proof that the full system is responsible. @Tbl-governance-assurance-lifecycle shows how that evidence becomes operational only when an owner can act on it and affected people have a path to contest a decision and obtain remedy.

At release time, @sec-ops-scale-end-to-end-evaluation-contract binds those assurance claims to the exact model, workload, acceptance authority, rollback target, and evidence-retention period. The assurance case explains why deployment is justified; the evaluation contract ensures that promotion and invalidation execute that judgment against one reproducible artifact.

| **Lifecycle stage**             | **Required artifact**                                                                                               | **Operational decision**                                                   |
|:--------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Context and affected parties    | Intended-use statement, prohibited uses, stakeholder map, decision-impact analysis                                  | Is this use legitimate and within organizational authority?                |
| Risk and requirements           | Harm model, legal and policy obligations, measurable acceptance criteria                                            | Which risks must be prevented, bounded, transferred, or accepted?          |
| Controls and dependencies       | Control inventory, supplier evidence, data and model lineage, tool permissions                                      | Are local and inherited controls sufficient for the operating envelope?    |
| Evaluation and assurance        | Assurance case, disaggregated results with uncertainty, robustness and security evidence, sustainability accounting | Does the evidence support launch, restricted launch, or rejection?         |
| Launch authority                | Signed decision record, residual-risk owner, rollback and appeal paths                                              | Who may authorize deployment, and who may stop it?                         |
| Operation and incident response | Monitoring thresholds, escalation owners, incident log, remedy workflow                                             | When must the system degrade, roll back, notify, compensate, or suspend?   |
| Material change                 | Change classification, impact assessment, revalidation scope                                                        | Does a new model, dataset, tool, region, or use invalidate prior approval? |
| Retirement                      | Decommission plan, retention and deletion record, user and dependent-system notice                                  | How are access, data, models, interfaces, and unresolved harms closed out? |

: **Governance and Assurance Lifecycle**: Responsible operation connects context and affected parties to requirements, inherited controls, evidence, launch authority, monitoring, incidents, remedy, material-change review, and retirement. Each stage produces an auditable artifact and a decision rather than a policy statement. {#tbl-governance-assurance-lifecycle tbl-colwidths="[18,40,42]"}

Named frameworks organize this work at different levels. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework\index{NIST AI RMF!core functions} structures activity around Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage; ISO/IEC 42001 specifies an organizational AI management system; ISO/IEC 23894 supplies AI risk-management guidance; and the OECD and UNESCO recommendations state broader principles and public responsibilities [@nist2023airmf; @isoiec420012023ai; @isoiec238942023ai; @oecd2024airecommendation; @unesco2022ethicsai]. @Tbl-responsible-ai-framework-crosswalk maps those perspectives onto the same operating lifecycle rather than treating them as interchangeable checklists.

| **Lifecycle responsibility**                       | **NIST AI RMF emphasis** | **Management-system and public-policy emphasis**                                           |
|:---------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Establish context, affected parties, and authority | Govern and Map           | Organizational context, leadership, stakeholder participation, and human oversight         |
| Measure risk and assemble evidence                 | Measure                  | Risk assessment, documented objectives, evaluation, transparency, and traceability         |
| Decide, operate, and respond                       | Manage                   | Operational controls, accountability, incident response, remedy, and continual improvement |
| Reassess change and retirement                     | Govern and Manage        | Change management, corrective action, lifecycle review, and decommissioning obligations    |

: **Framework Crosswalk**: Public frameworks differ in scope and legal status, but their durable systems contribution is complementary. They help organizations establish authority, identify and measure risk, operate controls, and reassess evidence through change and retirement. {#tbl-responsible-ai-framework-crosswalk tbl-colwidths="[28,24,48]"}

Three details keep this lifecycle from becoming ceremonial. First, fairness estimates must carry denominators, confidence intervals, and data-coverage limits; a noisy subgroup gap should trigger investigation, not automatic claims of either discrimination or safety. Second, sustainability evidence belongs in the same assurance record: the functional unit, system boundary, carbon signal, water accounting, embodied-impact allocation, uncertainty, and quality constraint determine whether an environmental claim is comparable or actionable. Third, systems that call tools or delegate actions need an authorization boundary independent of model alignment. Tool identities, least-privilege scopes, approval requirements, spend and rate limits, output validation, provenance, and revocation must be versioned and monitored because model-generated tool arguments and retrieved content remain untrusted inputs.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Lifecycle carbon accounting, functional units, and environmental footprints are formalized in @sec-sustainable-ai.
:::

The lifecycle also defines the boundary between fairness and alignment. Fairness asks how benefits, errors, opportunities, and burdens are distributed among affected people under competing normative criteria. Alignment asks whether an optimizing system pursues the objective and constraints its designers and legitimate stakeholders intended. An aligned system can implement an unfair objective faithfully, while a statistically fair classifier can still optimize the wrong social goal. Governance must evaluate both without collapsing one into the other.

Approval expires when its supporting assumptions no longer hold. A change of foundation model, training distribution, retrieval corpus, tool access, deployment region, user population, decision purpose, or human workflow can be *material* even when the application code is unchanged. The change record should identify which claims are invalidated and select the smallest defensible revalidation scope. At the end of service, retirement must revoke credentials, stop dependent interfaces safely, apply retention and deletion rules, preserve required audit evidence, notify affected users and downstream operators, and leave an owner for unresolved appeals or harms. Governance covers the system after launch and after shutdown, not only the moment a review board signs a release.

## Core Principles and the ML Lifecycle {#sec-responsible-ai-core-principles-1bd7}

A continuous integration pipeline can block a release when an evaluation detects a 15 percent drop in accuracy specifically for elderly users. Unlike a memory error, however, a subgroup result requires a specified population, sufficient evaluation data, and an agreed acceptance criterion. Responsible AI translates those commitments into deployment gates. The continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipeline enforces the approved rule, while the accountable reviewer interprets uncertainty and decides whether the evidence supports release, restricted use, or remediation.

Fairness can operate as a stability constraint\index{Fairness!stability constraint} on deployment policy, but it is not a general control-theoretic guarantee. Different criteria constrain selection rates, error rates, or the meaning of a score across population subgroups. Violations can compound through feedback loops, as in predictive policing, even while the service remains technically available. This principle encompasses both statistical metrics and broader normative concerns about equity, justice, and structural bias. The fairness analysis in @sec-responsible-ai-fairness-machine-learning-2ba4 examines the formal mathematical definitions in detail.

The same control-plane view makes explainability\index{Explainability!system evidence} one source of system evidence: attribution, examples, counterfactual analysis, and interpretable-model structure can expose patterns that human operators investigate [@phillips2020]. These methods do not reveal a model's complete causal reasoning, justify a decision, guarantee recourse, or prove that a safety constraint holds. Their value depends on a specified audience and decision: developers may need evidence for error analysis, auditors may need reproducible behavioral tests, and affected users may need understandable reasons plus a route to contest an outcome. Explanation therefore complements telemetry, documentation, evaluation, and human review rather than replacing them.

That observability must be paired with transparency\index{Transparency!lifecycle documentation}: openness about how AI systems are built, trained, validated, and deployed. Transparency includes disclosure of data sources, design assumptions, system limitations, and performance characteristics. While explainability focuses on understanding outputs, transparency addresses the broader lifecycle of the system.

Once system behavior is visible, accountability\index{Accountability!governance mechanisms} provides the mechanisms by which individuals or organizations are held responsible for AI outcomes. It involves traceability, documentation, auditing, and the ability to remedy harms. Accountability ensures that AI failures are not treated as abstract malfunctions but as consequences with real-world impact.

At the objective-function layer, value alignment\index{Value alignment!objective specification}[^fn-value-alignment-safety] asks whether AI systems pursue goals consistent with legitimate human intent and constraints. In practice, this involves technical challenges, including reward design and constraint specification, and broader questions about whose values are represented and enforced. Alignment does not subsume fairness: the former concerns fidelity to an objective, whereas the latter evaluates how outcomes and burdens are distributed and whether the objective itself is legitimate.

[^fn-value-alignment-safety]: **Value Alignment**\index{Value Alignment!AI safety}: The problem of ensuring AI systems optimize for human values rather than proxy objectives. Stuart Russell brought the problem to prominence in 2015, arguing that specifying objectives is harder than optimizing them. The engineering consequence is visible in recommender systems: a ranking objective built on engagement proxies such as clicks or expected watch time [@covington2016] can promote content that raises the proxy while degrading user welfare, so the objective itself becomes a governed artifact.

The lifecycle also needs human oversight\index{Human oversight!supervisory control}: the role of human judgment in supervising, correcting, or halting automated decisions. This includes humans in the loop[^fn-hitl-human-oversight] during operation, as well as organizational structures that ensure AI use remains accountable to societal values and real-world complexity.

[^fn-hitl-human-oversight]: **HITL (Human-in-the-Loop)**\index{Human-in-the-Loop!systems overhead}: A design pattern where humans actively participate in model decisions rather than being replaced by automation; the systems trade-off is latency vs. safety: HITL adds 100 ms to 30+ seconds per decision depending on domain. Large content-moderation systems have historically paired automated triage with thousands of human reviewers, demonstrating that the pattern scales only with proportional human infrastructure cost. In ML serving architectures, HITL requires routing logic, confidence thresholds for escalation, and queue management that fundamentally reshape the inference pipeline.

Privacy, robustness, and human oversight make the same point from different angles: principles alone do not ensure responsible systems. Translation from abstract ideals to concrete practice requires systematic integration across the ML lifecycle, where each principle manifests differently in data collection, model training, evaluation, deployment, and monitoring. The critical question is how these principles interact when they compete for priority.

### Integrating principles across the ML lifecycle {#sec-responsible-ai-integrating-principles-across-ml-lifecycle-7557}

Although the principles overlap, each creates a distinct engineering obligation, and each obligation acts in different phases of development. @Tbl-principles-lifecycle maps the responsible AI lifecycle\index{Responsible AI!lifecycle} across the major phases of ML system development: data collection, model training, evaluation, deployment, and monitoring.

| **Principle**      |   **Data Collection**   |     **Model Training**     |       **Evaluation**      |      **Deployment**      |      **Monitoring**      |
|:-------------------|:-----------------------:|:--------------------------:|:-------------------------:|:------------------------:|:------------------------:|
| **Fairness**       | Representative sampling |   Bias-aware algorithms    |    Group-level metrics    |   Threshold adjustment   |   Subgroup performance   |
| **Explainability** | Documentation standards | Interpretable architecture |  Model behavior analysis  | User-facing explanations | Explanation quality logs |
| **Transparency**   |   Data source tracking  |   Training documentation   |   Performance reporting   |       Model cards        |     Change tracking      |
| **Privacy**        |    Consent mechanisms   | Privacy-preserving methods | Privacy impact assessment |    Secure deployment     |    Access audit logs     |
| **Accountability** |  Governance frameworks  |      Decision logging      |    Audit trail creation   |   Override mechanisms    |    Incident tracking     |
| **Robustness**     |    Quality assurance    |  Robust training methods   |       Stress testing      |     Failure handling     |  Performance monitoring  |

: **Responsible AI Lifecycle**: Embedding fairness, explainability, privacy, accountability, and robustness throughout the ML system lifecycle, from data collection to monitoring, ensures these principles become architectural commitments rather than post hoc considerations. The table maps these principles to specific development phases, revealing how proactive integration addresses potential risks and promotes trustworthy AI systems. {#tbl-principles-lifecycle}

Fairness and privacy constraints begin at data collection; robustness and accountability become most critical during deployment and oversight. Explainability spans the full lifecycle, supporting model debugging at design time and user-facing justification at serving time. This mapping reinforces that responsible AI is a multiphase architectural commitment, not a post-hoc compliance step.

#### Resource requirements and equity implications {#sec-responsible-ai-resource-requirements-equity-implications-b967}

Implementing responsible AI principles requires computational resources that vary significantly across techniques and deployment contexts. These resource requirements create multifaceted equity considerations that extend beyond individual organizations to encompass broader social and environmental justice concerns. Organizations with limited computing budgets may be unable to implement comprehensive responsible AI protections, potentially creating disparate access to ethical safeguards. Large-scale model deployments that depend on accelerator clusters and low-latency connectivity can exclude users whose networks or devices cannot meet those assumptions.

Environmental justice concerns compound these access barriers through the engineering reality that responsible AI techniques impose energy and capacity costs. The concrete numbers later in the chapter are sizing assumptions for methods the chapter unpacks: differential privacy may require extra training iterations, real-time fairness monitoring consumes serving-path resources, and Shapley-value explanations can require many additional model evaluations unless they are approximated, cached, or generated asynchronously. These computational requirements translate directly into infrastructure demands: a high-traffic system serving these features to 10 million users must provision that overhead as additional capacity, sized with the ranges in @tbl-responsible-ai-overhead.

The geographic distribution of this computational infrastructure creates systematic inequities that engineers must consider in system design. Data centers supporting AI workloads concentrate in regions with low electricity costs and favorable regulations, areas that often correlate with lower-income communities that experience increased pollution, heat generation, and electrical grid strain while frequently lacking the high-bandwidth connectivity needed to access the AI services these facilities enable. This creates a feedback loop where computational equity depends not only on algorithmic design but on infrastructure placement decisions that affect both system performance and community welfare. The resource-overhead comparison later in this chapter quantifies the performance characteristics of specific responsible AI techniques.

### Transparency and explainability {#sec-responsible-ai-transparency-explainability-b137}

Machine learning systems are frequently criticized for their lack of interpretability. In many cases, models operate as opaque "black boxes," producing outputs that are difficult for users, developers, and regulators to understand or scrutinize. This opacity presents a significant barrier to trust, particularly in high-stakes domains such as criminal justice, healthcare, and finance, where accountability and the right to recourse are important. For example, ProPublica's evaluation of COMPAS, a recidivism-risk tool used in the United States, found racial disparities in false positive and false negative rates.[^fn-compas-disparate-impact] The proprietary nature of the system, combined with limited access to interpretability tools, hindered efforts to investigate or address the issue.

[^fn-compas-disparate-impact]: **COMPAS (Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions)**\index{COMPAS!algorithmic bias}: ProPublica's 2016 analysis found Black defendants were falsely flagged as future criminals at nearly twice the rate of white defendants (45 percent vs. 23 percent false positive rate). The proprietary, black-box nature of the system limited full inspection of model internals and training data, making the source of the observed error-rate disparity harder to investigate. Error-rate parity and predictive parity are distinct criteria, so the evaluation must name the criterion rather than treating one rate as a complete fairness verdict.

Explainability is the practice of producing evidence intended to help a specified audience understand aspects of a model's behavior. It includes both local explanations\index{Local explanation!prediction attribution}, which characterize influences or sensitivities around individual predictions, and global explanations\index{Global explanation!behavioral patterns}, which summarize broader behavioral patterns. An attribution describes how a method assigns influence under its assumptions; it is not automatically a causal explanation, a normative justification, or a feasible path to recourse. Transparency, by contrast, encompasses openness about the broader system design and operation. This includes disclosure of data sources, feature engineering, model architectures, training procedures, evaluation protocols, known limitations, intended uses, system boundaries, and governance structures.

The importance of explainability and transparency extends beyond technical considerations to legal requirements. In many jurisdictions, these principles are legal obligations rather than optional guidance. Under GDPR, solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects trigger Article 22 safeguards and related transparency duties, including meaningful information about the logic involved under access and notice provisions, subject to statutory exceptions [@gdpr2016; @edpb2018automatedProfiling].[^fn-gdpr-article-22] Similar regulatory pressures in other domains reinforce the need to treat explainability and transparency as core architectural requirements.

[^fn-gdpr-article-22]: **GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) Article 22**\index{GDPR!Article 22}: Article 22 gives data subjects protections against decisions based solely on automated processing that produce legal or similarly significant effects, with exceptions for contract necessity, authorization by law, or explicit consent plus safeguards [@gdpr2016]. Related notice and access provisions, including Article 15, require meaningful information about the logic involved for qualifying automated decision-making, and EDPB guidance treats those duties as part of a broader profiling and automated-decision governance regime [@edpb2018automatedProfiling]. For ML systems, this creates an architectural constraint: high-stakes automated-decision systems need explanation, recourse, and governance infrastructure rather than opaque serving-only APIs.

Implementing these principles requires anticipating the needs of different stakeholders, whose competing values and priorities are examined comprehensively in @sec-responsible-ai-normative-pluralism-value-conflicts-d61f. Designing for explainability and transparency therefore necessitates decisions about how and where to surface relevant information across the system lifecycle.

Transparency and explainability also support system reliability over time. As models are retrained or updated, mechanisms for interpretability and traceability allow detection of unexpected behavior, enable root cause analysis, and support governance. Embedded into the structure and operation of a system, these mechanisms provide the foundation for trust, oversight, and alignment with institutional and societal expectations.

While transparency and explainability enable stakeholders to understand system behavior, they do not guarantee that this behavior is equitable. A model can be fully transparent about how it makes decisions while still systematically disadvantaging certain groups. This distinction motivates the examination of fairness as a separate, complementary principle.

### Fairness in machine learning {#sec-responsible-ai-fairness-machine-learning-2ba4}

Automated decisions in hiring, lending, and healthcare affect millions of people, and historical data used to train these systems encodes decades of structural inequality. The engineering question is how to formalize "equitable treatment" in a way that a system can measure and enforce.

::: {#dfn-responsible-ai-algorithmic-fairness .callout-definition title="Algorithmic fairness"}

***Algorithmic fairness***\index{Algorithmic Fairness!definition} is a family of criteria for evaluating equitable treatment and outcomes in automated decisions. The group-based criteria developed here compare selection rates, errors, or score meaning across protected demographic groups; individual and causal criteria ask different questions.

1.  **Significance**: It transforms fairness from an intuition into a multi-objective optimization problem. Achieving fairness often requires trading off total accuracy for group-specific calibration\index{Calibration!group-specific}, where calibration is checked separately within each protected group. Such checks evaluate a chosen fairness criterion; they do not establish equitable treatment by themselves.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike average accuracy, which can hide subgroup disparities, group fairness examines the joint distribution of predictions and outcomes within each group, $p(\hat{Y},Y\mid A)$. The chosen criterion determines which conditional rates to compare; a group gap diagnoses that metric rather than fairness as a whole.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that there is a single "fair" solution. In reality, fairness requirements can conflict under specified assumptions\index{Fairness!incompatibility}. With unequal base rates, demographic parity and equalized odds can hold together only if each group's true positive rate equals its false positive rate, so the decision carries no information about the outcome. A constant classifier satisfies both; any informative classifier must give one up.

:::

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/responsible_ai_fairness_tax.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two columns comparing model accuracy. The unconstrained baseline column (gray) reaches 85 percent; the demographic-parity-constrained column (orange) reaches 81 percent, a 4-point fairness tax."}

*The illustrative policy incurs an accuracy cost; its size depends on the data and constraint.*
:::

Fairness in machine learning presents complex challenges that extend beyond transparency. The core requirement is that automated systems not disproportionately disadvantage protected groups. Because these systems are trained on historical data\index{Algorithmic bias!historical data}, they are susceptible to reproducing and amplifying patterns of systemic bias embedded in that data\index{Algorithmic bias!reproduction in training}. Without careful design, machine learning systems may unintentionally reinforce social inequities rather than mitigate them.

A widely studied example comes from the healthcare domain. An algorithm[^fn-healthcare-algorithm-bias] used to allocate care management resources in US hospitals was found to systematically underestimate the health needs of Black patients [@obermeyer2019]. The model used healthcare expenditures as a proxy for health status, but due to longstanding disparities in access and spending, Black patients were less likely to incur high costs. As a result, the model inferred that they were less sick, despite often having equal or greater medical need. This case illustrates how seemingly neutral design choices such as proxy variable selection\index{Algorithmic bias!proxy variable selection} can yield discriminatory outcomes when historical inequities are not properly accounted for. Correcting an invalid proxy can improve alignment with the actual clinical goal. A separate engineering question is whether imposing a particular fairness constraint reduces accuracy on a fixed target; the illustrative example below calls that scenario-specific reduction the fairness tax\index{Fairness!tax}.

[^fn-healthcare-algorithm-bias]: **Healthcare Algorithm Scale**\index{Healthcare Algorithm!scale}\index{Healthcare Algorithm!proxy bias}: The study examined one widely used algorithm in a broader class of risk-prediction tools that industry estimates placed at approximately 200 million U.S. patients annually [@obermeyer2019]. In the study's simulated correction at the automatic-enrollment threshold, the fraction of Black patients among those identified for additional care rose from 17.7 percent to 46.5 percent. These are shares of the selected population, not the fraction of all Black patients identified or a measured nationwide enrollment reduction.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fairness-tax-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE FAIRNESS TAX (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-responsible-ai-fairness-machine-learning-2ba4
# │
# │ Goal: Quantify the accuracy loss from enforcing demographic parity.
# │ Show: 4 percentage-point accuracy drop (85% -> 81%) when equalizing approval rates.
# │ How: Compare unconstrained accuracy vs parity-constrained accuracy.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_percent, fmt_pp

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class FairnessTaxAnalysis:
    """Quantify the cost of algorithmic fairness constraints."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    acc_baseline = 85.0
    acc_constrained = 81.0
    group_a_default_pct = 20
    group_b_default_pct = 40
    default_prob_threshold = 30
    group_a_approval_pct = 80
    group_b_approval_unconstrained_pct = 60
    default_prob_threshold_parity = 50

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    fairness_tax = acc_baseline - acc_constrained
    fairness_tax_relative = fairness_tax / acc_baseline * 100

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(fairness_tax - 4.0) < 0.01, f"Expected 4.0 pp fairness tax, got {fairness_tax}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    acc_unconstrained_str = fmt_percent(round(acc_baseline) / 100, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    acc_parity_str = fmt_percent(round(acc_constrained) / 100, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    fairness_tax_pp_str = fmt_pp(fairness_tax, precision=0, commas=False)
    fairness_tax_relative_pct_str = fmt_percent(fairness_tax_relative / 100, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
    group_a_default_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(group_a_default_pct) / 100, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    group_b_default_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(group_b_default_pct) / 100, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    default_prob_threshold_str = fmt_percent(round(default_prob_threshold) / 100, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    group_a_approval_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(group_a_approval_pct) / 100, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    group_b_approval_unconstrained_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(group_b_approval_unconstrained_pct) / 100, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    default_prob_threshold_parity_str = fmt_percent(round(default_prob_threshold_parity) / 100, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
```

The fairness-tax calculation isolates one criterion: demographic parity, which requires equal positive decision rates across groups. It does not represent every fairness goal; it shows the system cost of enforcing that criterion before the section compares demographic parity with equalized odds and equality of opportunity.

```{=latex}
\newpage
```

::: {#nbk-responsible-ai-fairness-tax .callout-notebook title="The fairness tax"}

**Problem**: Consider a credit model with `{python} FairnessTaxAnalysis.acc_unconstrained_str` accuracy. Group A (majority) has a `{python} FairnessTaxAnalysis.group_a_default_pct_str` default rate. Group B (minority) has a `{python} FairnessTaxAnalysis.group_b_default_pct_str` default rate due to systemic factors. If demographic parity (equal approval rates) is enforced, what happens to accuracy?

**Math**:

The approval-rate facts define the policy change; the scenario's accuracy values are assumed held-out validation results, where the additional Group B approvals carry higher default risk.

1.  **Unconstrained**: Model approves everyone with predicted default prob < `{python} FairnessTaxAnalysis.default_prob_threshold_str`.
    *   Group A approval: `{python} FairnessTaxAnalysis.group_a_approval_pct_str`.
    *   Group B approval: `{python} FairnessTaxAnalysis.group_b_approval_unconstrained_pct_str`.
    *   Total Accuracy: `{python} FairnessTaxAnalysis.acc_unconstrained_str`.
2.  **Constrained (parity)**: Must approve Group B at `{python} FairnessTaxAnalysis.group_a_approval_pct_str` rate.
    *   New threshold for Group B: Approve default prob < `{python} FairnessTaxAnalysis.default_prob_threshold_parity_str`.
    *   This forces the model to approve many risky applicants in Group B.
    *   New Total Accuracy: `{python} FairnessTaxAnalysis.acc_parity_str`.

**Systems insight**: Fairness is not free. Enforcing parity cost `{python} FairnessTaxAnalysis.fairness_tax_pp_str` of accuracy (about a `{python} FairnessTaxAnalysis.fairness_tax_relative_pct_str` relative accuracy drop in this credit-scoring scenario). In this scenario that drop is the fairness tax. Because accuracy is scored against historical default labels that may themselves reflect the systemic factors in the problem, the tax measures disagreement with past outcomes, not necessarily a loss of true predictive quality.

:::

Practitioners need formal methods to evaluate fairness given these risks of perpetuating bias. The fairness gates of @sec-ml-operations-scale-fairness-gates-145c already encode two such criteria, demographic parity (@eq-demographic-parity) and equalized odds (@eq-equalized-odds), as release thresholds. This section examines what each criterion measures, adds equality of opportunity and calibration, and shows why the criteria conflict. Before developing them, it helps to frame the notation as a way to express competing fairness goals, not as a proof exercise.

::: {#psp-responsible-ai-fairness-notation-engineering-vocabulary .callout-perspective title="Fairness notation as engineering vocabulary"}

Before examining formal definitions, the fundamental challenge is that fairness can mean different operational constraints. A system may treat everyone identically, account for different baseline conditions, optimize equal outcomes, preserve equal opportunity, or enforce equal treatment. These choices lead to different mathematical criteria, each capturing a different aspect of fairness.

The next subsections introduce formal fairness definitions using probability notation. These metrics (demographic parity, equalized odds, equality of opportunity) appear throughout ML fairness literature and shape regulatory frameworks. Focus on understanding the intuition: what each metric measures and why it matters, rather than mathematical proofs. The concrete examples after each definition illustrate practical application. If probability notation is unfamiliar, start with the verbal descriptions and return to the formal definitions later.

:::

Suppose a model $h(x)$ predicts a binary outcome, such as loan repayment, and let $A$ represent a sensitive attribute with subgroups $a$ and $b$. The field uses three widely adopted fairness definitions:

#### Demographic parity {#sec-responsible-ai-demographic-parity-f126}

::: {#dfn-responsible-ai-demographic-parity .callout-definition title="Demographic parity"}

***Demographic parity***\index{Demographic Parity!definition} is the fairness constraint where a model's positive prediction rate is independent of group membership $(\Pr(h(x)=1 \mid A=a) = \Pr(h(x)=1 \mid A=b))$.

1.  **Significance**: It requires equal positive prediction rates across groups, regardless of underlying base-rate differences. It does not require identical outcomes for every individual, and it is not universally more restrictive than error-rate or calibration criteria.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike Equalized Odds (which focuses on error rates like False Positives), Demographic Parity focuses only on the Final Prediction\index{Demographic Parity!final prediction}, ignoring the relationship between the prediction and the ground truth.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that Demographic Parity ensures "fairness." In reality, it can force the model to sacrifice Calibration\index{Calibration!fairness trade-off}: to meet the parity constraint, the model may have to intentionally misclassify qualified individuals in one group or unqualified individuals in another.

:::

Demographic parity asks whether favorable outcomes, such as loan approval or treatment referral, occur at equal rates across subgroups defined by a sensitive attribute $A$. Formally, the model satisfies demographic parity if:
$$
\Pr\big(h(x) = 1 \mid A = a\big) = \Pr\big(h(x) = 1 \mid A = b\big)
$$

In the healthcare example, this criterion would ask whether Black and white patients were referred for care at the same rate, regardless of their underlying health needs. That may sound like equal access, but it ignores real differences in medical status and risk, potentially overcorrecting when needs are not evenly distributed. The limitation of ignoring base-rate differences motivates more nuanced fairness criteria.

#### Equalized odds {#sec-responsible-ai-equalized-odds-6570}

Equalized odds\index{Equalized odds!error-rate parity} requires that the model's predictions are conditionally independent of group membership given the true label. Specifically, the true positive and false positive rates must be equal across groups:
$$
\Pr\big(h(x) = 1 \mid A = a, Y = y\big) = \Pr\big(h(x) = 1 \mid A = b, Y = y\big), \quad \text{for } y \in \{0, 1\}.
$$

That is, for each true outcome $Y = y$, the model should produce the same prediction distribution across groups $A = a$ and $A = b$. The model should therefore behave similarly across groups for individuals with the same true outcome, whether they qualify for a positive result or not. It ensures that errors (both missed and incorrect positives) are distributed equally.

Applied to the medical case, equalized odds would ensure that patients with the same actual health needs (the true label $Y$) are equally likely to be correctly or incorrectly referred, regardless of race. The original algorithm violated this by under-referring Black patients who were equally or more sick than their white counterparts, highlighting unequal true positive rates.

#### Equality of opportunity {#sec-responsible-ai-equality-opportunity-1c3d}

Equality of opportunity\index{Equality of opportunity!true-positive rate} is a less stringent relaxation of equalized odds that focuses only on the true positive rate [@hardt2016equality]. It requires that, among individuals who should receive a positive outcome, the probability of receiving one is equal across groups:
$$
\Pr\big(h(x) = 1 \mid A = a, Y = 1\big) = \Pr\big(h(x) = 1 \mid A = b, Y = 1\big).
$$

Equality of opportunity ensures that qualified individuals, who have $Y = 1$, are treated equally by the model regardless of group membership.

In the running example, this measure would ensure that among patients who do require care, both Black and white individuals have an equal chance of being identified by the model. In the case of the US hospital system, the algorithm's use of healthcare expenditure as a proxy variable led to a failure in meeting this criterion: Black patients with significant health needs were less likely to receive care due to their lower historical spending. The following worked example introduces a separate loan decision scenario to calculate all three criteria, showing why a single model can fail each fairness test in a different way.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fairness-worked-example-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CALCULATING FAIRNESS METRICS — WORKED EXAMPLE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the "Calculating fairness metrics" worked-example callout below.
# │
# │ Goal: Derive the demographic-parity and equal-opportunity disparities and the
# │       group error rates from the 200-applicant loan scenario.
# │ Show: parity gap (0.30), TPR gap (0.29), TPR per group (89/60 percent), and
# │       FPR per group (55/20 percent).
# │ How: Load the per-group confusion counts (scenario), derive each rate and gap.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_math, fmt_percent, fmt_pp

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class FairnessWorkedExample:
    """All three fairness criteria on the 200-applicant loan scenario."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Per-group confusion counts, scenario inputs) ────────────
    # Group A (100 applicants): approved 70 (40 repaid, 30 default);
    #                           rejected 30 (5 would repay, 25 default)
    a_approved, a_total = 70, 100
    a_tp, a_fn = 40, 5  # would-repay applicants: approved vs rejected
    a_fp, a_tn = 30, 25  # would-default applicants: approved vs rejected
    # Group B (100 applicants): approved 40 (30 repaid, 10 default);
    #                           rejected 60 (20 would repay, 40 default)
    b_approved, b_total = 40, 100
    b_tp, b_fn = 30, 20
    b_fp, b_tn = 10, 40

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    approval_a = a_approved / a_total  # 0.70
    approval_b = b_approved / b_total  # 0.40
    parity_gap = approval_a - approval_b  # 0.30
    tpr_a = a_tp / (a_tp + a_fn)  # 0.89
    tpr_b = b_tp / (b_tp + b_fn)  # 0.60
    tpr_gap = round(tpr_a, 2) - tpr_b  # 0.29 (from displayed TPRs)
    fpr_a = a_fp / (a_fp + a_tn)  # 0.55
    fpr_b = b_fp / (b_fp + b_tn)  # 0.20

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    check(a_total == a_approved + 30 and b_total == b_approved + 60, "Approved + rejected must equal each group's applicant total")
    check(parity_gap > 0 and tpr_gap > 0, "Both disparities favor Group A")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    parity_gap_str = fmt(parity_gap, precision=2, commas=False)
    tpr_gap_str = fmt(tpr_gap, precision=2, commas=False)
    parity_gap_math = fmt_math(r"0.70 - 0.40 = " + parity_gap_str)
    tpr_gap_math = fmt_math(r"0.89 - 0.60 = " + tpr_gap_str)
    parity_gap_pp_attr_str = fmt_pp(parity_gap * 100, precision=0, style="prose", attributive=True)
    tpr_gap_pp_attr_str = fmt_pp(tpr_gap * 100, precision=0, style="prose", attributive=True)
    tpr_a_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(tpr_a, 2), precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    tpr_b_pct_str = fmt_percent(tpr_b, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    fpr_a_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(fpr_a, 2), precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    fpr_b_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(fpr_b, 2), precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
```

::: {#nbk-responsible-ai-calculating-fairness-metrics .callout-notebook title="Calculating fairness metrics"}

**Problem**: Calculate Demographic Parity across two demographic groups (100 applicants each) for a loan approval model.

**Variables**:

- Group A: 70 approved (40 repaid, 30 defaulted), 30 rejected.
- Group B: 40 approved (30 repaid, 10 defaulted), 60 rejected.

**Math**:

1. **Group A approval rate**: $\Pr(h(x) = 1 \mid A = a) = \frac{70}{100} = 0.70$.
2. **Group B approval rate**: $\Pr(h(x) = 1 \mid A = b) = \frac{40}{100} = 0.40$.
3. **Parity gap**: `{python} FairnessWorkedExample.parity_gap_math` (`{python} FairnessWorkedExample.parity_gap_pp_attr_str` gap).

**Systems insight**: Evaluating Demographic Parity exposes group approval rate disparities regardless of ground-truth repayment capability, requiring explicit metric selection during model threshold calibration.

:::

The next calculation assumes that repayment labels are also known for rejected applicants: among the rejected applicants in Group A, five would repay and 25 would default; in Group B, 20 would repay and 40 would default. These are hypothetical evaluation labels. A production lender ordinarily observes repayment only for approved loans, so estimating the same error rates requires additional evidence about rejected applicants and an account of how that evidence was obtained.

::: {#nbk-responsible-ai-equality-of-opportunity .callout-notebook title="Calculating equality of opportunity"}

**Calculating equality of opportunity (true positive rate [TPR])**:

Among applicants who *would actually repay* ($Y=1$):
\begin{gather*}
\Pr(h(x) = 1 \mid A = a, Y = 1) = \frac{40}{40 + 5} = \frac{40}{45} \approx 0.89
\\
\Pr(h(x) = 1 \mid A = b, Y = 1) = \frac{30}{30 + 20} = \frac{30}{50} = 0.60
\end{gather*}

**Disparity**: `{python} FairnessWorkedExample.tpr_gap_math` (`{python} FairnessWorkedExample.tpr_gap_pp_attr_str` gap in TPR)

The model violates equality of opportunity: among qualified applicants who would repay, Group A members are correctly approved `{python} FairnessWorkedExample.tpr_a_pct_str` of the time while Group B members are only approved `{python} FairnessWorkedExample.tpr_b_pct_str` of the time.

**Calculating equalized odds (true positive rate [TPR] and false positive rate [FPR])**:

The TPR values are calculated in the preceding step. For false positive rates among applicants who *would not repay* ($Y=0$):
\begin{gather*}
\Pr(h(x) = 1 \mid A = a, Y = 0) = \frac{30}{30 + 25} = \frac{30}{55} \approx 0.55
\\
\Pr(h(x) = 1 \mid A = b, Y = 0) = \frac{10}{10 + 40} = \frac{10}{50} = 0.20
\end{gather*}

The model also has unequal false positive rates: it incorrectly approves `{python} FairnessWorkedExample.fpr_a_pct_str` of Group A applicants who will default, but only `{python} FairnessWorkedExample.fpr_b_pct_str` of Group B applicants who will default. This reveals the model is more "generous" with Group A even when they will not repay.

**Systems insight**: This model violates all three fairness criteria. Addressing one criterion does not automatically satisfy others. Whether they can all be satisfied together depends on base rates and prediction quality, the question the impossibility results address next.

:::

The loan approval example shows that this particular model violates all three criteria. That observation alone does not prove that satisfying them together is impossible. Impossibility results require additional conditions on base rates, prediction quality, and the criteria being combined; those conditions determine which trade-offs the deployment must resolve.

These definitions capture different aspects of fairness and can conflict under deployment-specific constraints.[^fn-fairness-impossibility-theorem] A university admissions example illustrates one such tension before the broader calibration and error-rate results [@kleinberg2016inherent; @chouldechova2017].

[^fn-fairness-impossibility-theorem]: **Fairness Impossibility Theorems**\index{Fairness!impossibility theorems}: @kleinberg2016inherent studies groupwise score calibration together with balance of mean scores in each outcome class. @chouldechova2017 studies predictive parity and error-rate constraints for recidivism prediction. These are distinct conditions; their incompatibility results require assumptions on base rates and predictive performance. Demographic parity is a distinct constraint on selection rates that can also conflict with calibration or error-rate goals in practice. The systems consequence is fundamental: no amount of engineering can satisfy every normative fairness criterion in all settings, so fairness becomes a constrained multi-objective optimization requiring explicit policy choices about which criterion to prioritize for a given deployment context.

Goal 1 (Demographic Parity) would be to admit students so that the admitted class reflects the demographics of the applicant pool, perhaps 50 percent from Group A and 50 percent from Group B. Goal 2 (Equal Opportunity) would be to ensure that among all qualified applicants, the admission rate is the same across groups, so that 80 percent of qualified Group A applicants get in and 80 percent of qualified Group B applicants get in. If only qualified applicants are admitted and qualification rates differ, the second policy produces different overall admission rates. Equalizing those rates then requires changing the qualified-applicant admission rates or admitting some unqualified applicants. The conflict arises because the policy admits no unqualified applicants; without that restriction, both goals can be met by admitting some unqualified applicants from the group with fewer qualified ones. The broader trade-offs in @fig-fairness-impossibility require an explicit value judgment about which criteria and decision constraints to prioritize.

The fairness impossibility law (principle \ref{pri-fairness-impossibility}) concerns an additional combination of requirements. Calibration requires a risk score to retain its probability meaning within each group. The score-balance theorem additionally requires equal average scores across groups among people with positive outcomes and, separately, among people with negative outcomes. With unequal base rates and imperfect prediction, all three requirements cannot hold together. This is not a claim that a calibrated score can never yield equalized odds at a particular threshold; demographic parity adds another, separate selection-rate constraint. Satisfying one criterion may preclude another, so engineers must treat fairness metrics like latency budgets, explicit trade-offs chosen by stakeholders, enforced by the system, and monitored for violation. Determining which metric to prioritize requires careful consideration of the application context, potential harms, and stakeholder values as detailed in @sec-responsible-ai-normative-pluralism-value-conflicts-d61f [@barocas-hardt-narayanan].

::: {#fig-fairness-impossibility fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Conditional Fairness Trade-Offs**: For score-based prediction, calibration within groups and equal mean scores within both outcome classes cannot all hold with unequal base rates and imperfect prediction. Equal base rates or perfect prediction are exceptional cases. This score-balance theorem is distinct from checking equalized odds at one decision threshold." fig-alt="Three score conditions feed a joint feasibility check, with unequal base rates and imperfect prediction marked infeasible; equal base rates or perfect prediction are exceptions."}
![](images/svg/fairness-impossibility.svg)

:::

@Fig-fairness-metric-disagreement makes this trade-off concrete by sweeping a classification threshold across a synthetic scenario with differing group base rates. Across the evaluated nontrivial operating range, at least one of the plotted selection-rate or error-rate metrics is substantially violated, illustrating the broader operational lesson that fairness criteria can conflict and require explicit prioritization.

::: {#fig-fairness-metric-disagreement fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Fairness Metric Disagreement Across Thresholds**: Three fairness metrics, demographic parity, equalized odds, and equal opportunity, computed on a classifier with differing group base rates as the classification threshold varies over a nontrivial operating range. At every evaluated threshold, at least one metric is substantially violated, illustrating practical trade-offs among selection-rate, error-rate, and opportunity criteria. Trivial always-positive or always-negative classifiers fall outside the evaluated range." fig-alt="Line plot showing three fairness metrics varying over a nontrivial classification-threshold range. No evaluated threshold brings all three metrics to zero simultaneously."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ FAIRNESS METRIC DISAGREEMENT (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-fairness-metric-disagreement—Chouldechova-Kleinberg
# │
# │ Goal: Plot DP, Equalized Odds, Equal Opportunity vs threshold over a
# │       nontrivial operating range.
# │ Show: Three curves; threshold sweep; impossibility illustration.
# │ How: Synthetic scores_a/b, labels_a/b; compute metrics per threshold;
# │      book_style.setup_plot().
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# ┌── 1. CANVAS ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Plot DP, Equalized Odds, Equal Opportunity vs threshold; show no
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from binder.tools.figures import style as book_style

fig, ax, COLORS, plt = book_style.setup_plot(figsize=(8, 5))

# ┌── 2. ARRAYS ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
np.random.seed(42)
n_per_group = 5000

# Group A: higher base rate (60% positive), scores ~ Beta(3,2)
# Group B: lower base rate (30% positive), scores ~ Beta(2,3)
scores_a = np.random.beta(3, 2, n_per_group)
scores_b = np.random.beta(2, 3, n_per_group)

# True labels: Pr(Y=1) correlated with score
labels_a = (np.random.rand(n_per_group) < scores_a * 0.85 + 0.15).astype(int)
labels_b = (np.random.rand(n_per_group) < scores_b * 0.55 + 0.05).astype(int)

thresholds = np.linspace(0.15, 0.85, 50)
dp_diff = []
eo_diff = []
eqopp_diff = []

# ┌── 3. RENDER ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
for t in thresholds:
    pred_a = (scores_a >= t).astype(int)
    pred_b = (scores_b >= t).astype(int)

    # Demographic Parity Difference: |Pr(Yhat=1|A) - Pr(Yhat=1|B)|
    dp = abs(pred_a.mean() - pred_b.mean())
    dp_diff.append(dp)

    # True Positive Rates
    tpr_a = pred_a[labels_a == 1].mean() if labels_a.sum() > 0 else 0
    tpr_b = pred_b[labels_b == 1].mean() if labels_b.sum() > 0 else 0

    # False Positive Rates
    fpr_a = pred_a[labels_a == 0].mean() if (labels_a == 0).sum() > 0 else 0
    fpr_b = pred_b[labels_b == 0].mean() if (labels_b == 0).sum() > 0 else 0

    # Equal Opportunity Difference: |TPR_A - TPR_B|
    eqopp = abs(tpr_a - tpr_b)
    eqopp_diff.append(eqopp)

    # Equalized Odds Difference: |TPR_A - TPR_B| + |FPR_A - FPR_B|
    eo = abs(tpr_a - tpr_b) + abs(fpr_a - fpr_b)
    eo_diff.append(eo)

ax.plot(thresholds, dp_diff, color=COLORS['BlueLine'], linewidth=2, label='Demographic Parity', zorder=3)
ax.plot(thresholds, eo_diff, color=COLORS['OrangeLine'], linewidth=2, label='Equalized Odds', zorder=3)
ax.plot(thresholds, eqopp_diff, color=COLORS['GreenLine'], linewidth=2, label='Equal Opportunity', zorder=3)

# Perfect fairness reference
ax.axhline(y=0, color=COLORS['secondary'], linestyle='--', linewidth=1, alpha=0.6)

# Check if there is any threshold where all three are below 0.05
dp_arr = np.array(dp_diff)
eo_arr = np.array(eo_diff)
eqopp_arr = np.array(eqopp_diff)
max_violation = np.maximum(np.maximum(dp_arr, eo_arr), eqopp_arr)

# ┌── 4. DECORATE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ax.annotate(
    'No evaluated\noperating threshold\nsatisfies all\nthree metrics',
    xy=(thresholds[np.argmin(max_violation)], max_violation[np.argmin(max_violation)]),
    xytext=(0.79, 0.40),
    fontsize=8,
    ha='center',
    va='center',
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color=COLORS['primary'], shrinkB=5, lw=0.75),
    color=COLORS['primary'],
    fontweight='normal',
    bbox=dict(boxstyle='round,pad=0.35', facecolor='white', edgecolor=COLORS['secondary'], lw=0.8, alpha=0.95),
)

ax.set_xlabel('Classification threshold')
ax.set_ylabel('Fairness metric violation (0 = perfect fairness)')
ax.set_xlim(0.15, 0.85)
ax.set_ylim(-0.02, 0.65)
plt.legend(
    loc='upper left',
    fontsize=8,
    frameon=True,
    facecolor='white',
    framealpha=0.95,
    edgecolor=COLORS['secondary'],
    fancybox=True,
    borderpad=0.6,
)
plt.show()
plt.close()
```

:::

Recognizing these tensions, operational systems must treat fairness as a constraint that informs decisions throughout the machine learning lifecycle. It is shaped by how data are collected and represented, how objectives and proxies are selected, how model predictions are thresholded, and how feedback mechanisms are structured. For example, a choice between ranking vs. classification models can yield different patterns of access across groups, even when using the same underlying data.

Fairness metrics help formalize equity goals but are often limited to predefined demographic categories. In practice, these categories may be too coarse to capture the full range of disparities present in real-world data.

#### Observational and causal fairness {#sec-responsible-ai-causal-fairness}

The preceding metrics describe associations in observed decisions: selection rates, error rates, or calibration differ across groups. They can establish a disparity without identifying the pathway that produced it. The same approval-rate gap could arise from direct use of a protected attribute, a correlated proxy, unequal access to an earlier process, measurement error, or an unobserved common cause. No comparison of observed rates alone distinguishes these mechanisms.

A causal claim adds a structural causal model\index{Structural causal model!fairness} whose arrows state how protected attribute $A$, mediators $M$, outcome $Y$, and decision $\widehat Y$ are assumed to relate. **Counterfactual fairness**\index{Counterfactual fairness!definition} then asks whether the decision for the same individual, holding the modeled background factors fixed, would have changed in a counterfactual world where $A$ had taken another value [@kusner2017counterfactual]. This is a question about an assumed data-generating process, not a stronger version of demographic parity.

The healthcare proxy illustrates the distinction. A graph might include race $A \rightarrow$ access to care $M \rightarrow$ expenditure $X \rightarrow$ risk score $\widehat Y$, alongside pathways from health need $Y$ to expenditure. A total effect\index{Causal effect!total, fairness} asks how changing $A$ propagates through every modeled path. A path-specific effect\index{Causal effect!path-specific, fairness} isolates selected routes, such as the historically mediated access-to-expenditure path [@nabi2018fair]. Declaring one path permissible and another discriminatory is a domain and normative judgment; neither the graph nor the estimator makes that choice automatically.

Causal conclusions require assumptions that observational data\index{Counterfactual fairness!observational limitations} alone cannot establish: which variables and arrows belong in the graph, whether relevant confounders are measured, and whether the counterfactual interventions are coherent. Different plausible structures can support different answers. Causal analysis therefore complements group metrics, domain knowledge, legal analysis, and stakeholder participation. The metrics continue to monitor realized disparities; the causal model makes the additional mechanism claim and its assumptions inspectable.

#### Intersectional fairness {#sec-responsible-ai-intersectional-fairness-af99}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: gender-shades-intersection
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ GENDER SHADES INTERSECTIONAL GAP (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-responsible-ai-intersectional-fairness-af99
# │
# │ Goal: Pin the IBM Gender Shades subgroup accuracies to the registry.
# │ Show: "99.7 percent" (lighter-skinned men) vs "65.3 percent" (darker-skinned women).
# │ How: Read Literature.Fairness (percent values).
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_percent

class GenderShadesIntersection:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    light_male_pct = float(Literature.Fairness.GenderShadesIbmAccuracyLightMale)
    dark_female_pct = float(Literature.Fairness.GenderShadesIbmAccuracyDarkFemale)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    gap_pp = light_male_pct - dark_female_pct

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(30 < gap_pp < 40, f"Gender Shades IBM light-male vs dark-female gap should be about 34 points, got {gap_pp:.1f}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    light_male_pct_str = fmt_percent(light_male_pct / 100, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
    dark_female_pct_str = fmt_percent(dark_female_pct / 100, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
```

A critical limitation of standard fairness analysis is that it often evaluates single axes of identity (for example, race or gender) independently. This can mask profound disparities that exist at the intersection of these attributes.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/responsible_ai_intersectional_quadrant.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="A labeled 2-by-2 skin-tone-by-gender grid. Most cells show high accuracy, while the dark-skinned women cell is crimson and marked 65 percent, showing the failing intersection hidden by single-axis audits."}

*Error concentrates at the intersection: dark-skinned women.*
:::

For example, IBM's gender-classification system achieved `{python} GenderShadesIntersection.light_male_pct_str` accuracy for lighter-skinned men but only `{python} GenderShadesIntersection.dark_female_pct_str` for darker-skinned women in the Gender Shades evaluation [@buolamwini2018gender]. A single-axis audit can obscure such an intersectional disparity. This phenomenon, sometimes called fairness gerrymandering\index{Fairness!gerrymandering}, requires evaluating model performance on intersectional subgroups (for example, $\text{Race}{\times}\text{Gender}$) to detect and mitigate compounded biases.

A principled approach to fairness must account for overlapping and intersectional identities, ensuring that model behavior remains consistent across subgroups that may not be explicitly labeled in advance. Recent work in this area emphasizes the need for predictive reliability across a wide range of population slices [@hebert2018multicalibration], reinforcing the idea that fairness must be considered a system-level requirement, not a localized adjustment. This expanded view of fairness highlights the importance of designing architectures, evaluation protocols, and monitoring strategies that support more nuanced, context-sensitive assessments of model behavior.

#### Quantitative fairness measurement {#sec-responsible-ai-quantitative-fairness-measurement-a8f2}

Formal fairness criteria become operational only when practitioners can measure the degree of violation and establish actionable thresholds for intervention. The resulting mathematical framework quantifies disparities and determines when they warrant corrective action.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fairness-metrics-table-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ FAIRNESS METRICS ON THE LOAN EXAMPLE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @tbl-responsible-ai-fairness-metrics and the paragraph below it.
# │
# │ Goal: Score the four group-fairness metrics on the running loan scenario.
# │ Show: Disparate impact ratio (0.57), statistical parity difference (0.30),
# │       equal opportunity difference (0.29), and average absolute odds
# │       difference (0.32).
# │ How: Load the displayed group rates (scenario inputs), derive each metric,
# │      and build the worked-arithmetic math spans for the "Loan value" column.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_math

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class FairnessMetricsTable:
    """Score the four group-fairness metrics on the loan example."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Scenario rates from the worked example) ─────────────────
    approval_a = 0.70  # Group A approval rate (70/100)
    approval_b = 0.40  # Group B approval rate (40/100)
    tpr_a_display = 0.89  # Group A true-positive rate (40/45, displayed)
    tpr_b_display = 0.60  # Group B true-positive rate (30/50)
    delta_fpr_display = 0.35  # |FPR_a - FPR_b| = |0.55 - 0.20|, displayed

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    di_ratio = min(approval_a, approval_b) / max(approval_a, approval_b)  # 0.57
    spd = approval_a - approval_b  # 0.30
    eod = tpr_a_display - tpr_b_display  # 0.29
    aod = 0.5 * (eod + delta_fpr_display)  # 0.32

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    check(di_ratio < 0.8, "Illustrative approval-rate ratio must remain below 0.8")
    check(0 < spd < 1 and 0 < eod < 1, "Additive gaps must be valid fractions")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    approval_a_str = fmt(approval_a, precision=2, commas=False)
    approval_b_str = fmt(approval_b, precision=2, commas=False)
    tpr_a_str = fmt(tpr_a_display, precision=2, commas=False)
    tpr_b_str = fmt(tpr_b_display, precision=2, commas=False)
    fpr_a_str = fmt(0.55, precision=2, commas=False)
    fpr_b_str = fmt(0.20, precision=2, commas=False)
    di_ratio_str = fmt(di_ratio, precision=2, commas=False)
    spd_str = fmt(spd, precision=2, commas=False)
    eod_str = fmt(eod, precision=2, commas=False)
    aod_str = fmt(aod, precision=2, commas=False)
    di_ratio_math = fmt_math(r"\dfrac{0.40}{0.70} = " + di_ratio_str)
    spd_math = fmt_math(r"0.70 - 0.40 = " + spd_str)
    eod_math = fmt_math(r"0.89 - 0.60 = " + eod_str)
    aod_math = fmt_math(r"\tfrac{1}{2}[0.29 + 0.35] = " + aod_str)
```
Four point metrics turn the fairness criteria introduced above into numbers an auditor can threshold. Each one equalizes a different quantity, so each exposes a different failure of the same classifier. @Tbl-responsible-ai-fairness-metrics defines them and scores them on the running loan example, where Group A is approved at `{python} FairnessMetricsTable.approval_a_str` and Group B at `{python} FairnessMetricsTable.approval_b_str`, qualified-applicant true-positive rates are `{python} FairnessMetricsTable.tpr_a_str` and `{python} FairnessMetricsTable.tpr_b_str`, and unqualified-applicant false-positive rates are `{python} FairnessMetricsTable.fpr_a_str` and `{python} FairnessMetricsTable.fpr_b_str`.

| **Metric**                                                                                                                                                 | **Equalizes**                                       | **Formula** $(a, b)$                                                                      |                 **Loan value**                | **Choose it when**                                                                             |
|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------:|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
